analysis.one_liner: Stops courts from sealing safety information that turns up in civil lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: after one committee referral and one subcommittee referral, it died in the House Judiciary Committee when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies settle lawsuits, courts often issue orders that keep what was uncovered in the case secret, even when the evidence points to a product defect, a drug hazard, or another danger to the public. This bill would have barred federal courts from approving such secrecy orders in cases involving public health or safety unless a judge made specific findings that secrecy was truly necessary, and it would have allowed parties to always report safety information to government regulators.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who buy products, take medicines, or live near hazards. Today, when a lawsuit exposes a safety problem, the company can settle on the condition that the evidence stays under seal, so the next customer, patient, or regulator never learns about it. The bill would have let judges keep records sealed only for a strong, specific reason, such as protecting a person's private financial or health information, which the bill singled out for protection. It would also have guaranteed that parties could always report hazards to federal or state agencies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, patients, and workers exposed to hidden hazards

how_it_helps.text: Bars courts from sealing discovery material, settlement terms, or court records in cases involving public health or safety unless the judge first makes specific findings that secrecy would not hide a hazard, or that a specific and substantial interest outweighs the public's interest in knowing [S2] [S3].

Prohibits enforcing any settlement term that stops a party from reporting information to a federal or state agency with authority over the activity in question, so regulators always hear about dangers uncovered in litigation [S2] [S3].
Puts the burden of proof on whoever wants the secrecy order, and blocks parties from demanding secrecy stipulations as a condition of settling [S2] [S3].

Protects legitimate privacy: it creates a presumption that a person's own financial or health information outweighs public disclosure, and it expressly leaves classified information and existing confidentiality rules untouched [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations facing lawsuits over product safety, including drug makers, automakers, and other manufacturers, would lose their ability to settle quietly with the evidence sealed, making some cases more expensive to resolve and making their litigation conduct more public. Trade-secret holders would also face a stricter federal standard for keeping confidential business information sealed, even though the bill preserves existing confidentiality protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate defendants and trade-secret holders in lawsuits

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that a one-size-fits-all federal rule replaces judges' case-by-case judgment. Courts already weigh secrecy requests under their own rules, and critics of this type of legislation have argued that a blanket statute could make settlement harder, push more cases to trial, and raise costs for everyone involved in civil litigation.

Some confidential business information, such as trade secrets, would face a higher bar for sealing, which companies argue could force them to disclose competitively sensitive material in cases where the safety issue is disputed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and concrete: the public learns about safety hazards that would otherwise stay hidden under court seal, and regulators are guaranteed to hear about them. The cost falls mainly on defendants, who lose a settlement tool and face a stricter standard for confidentiality, though the bill was drafted to keep protecting personal privacy, trade secrets through existing rules, and classified information. The main design risk is the loss of judicial flexibility, which is a genuine but modest cost compared with the hazard of never learning that a product or drug is dangerous.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, a New York Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, introduced the bill on May 26, 2010 [S1] [S3].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and on July 26, 2010 referred it further to the Subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy [S5].
No further action was recorded, and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate defendants keep their current ability to settle lawsuits with safety evidence sealed, so hazards that surface in litigation remain undisclosed to the public and regulators.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate defendants who settle with the evidence sealed

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition is recorded in the congressional record; the bill drew no cosponsors of either party and died without a hearing.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants in product liability suits (drug makers, automakers, consumer product manufacturers)
industries.note: These companies use court-approved protective orders and confidentiality terms to settle cases without the underlying safety evidence becoming public. The bill would have ended that practice in health-and-safety cases, meaning hazards found in discovery would reach customers, workers, and regulators. Its interest in quiet settlements runs against the public's interest in knowing about dangers.

industries.industry: Trade-secret holders and litigants relying on confidential business information
industries.note: The bill sets a higher bar for sealing business information in health-and-safety cases, while preserving existing confidentiality protections and adding a strong presumption protecting individuals' personal financial and health data. Companies lose some secrecy; some of that secrecy was protecting genuinely sensitive information rather than hazards.

Confidential settlements are a core tool for resolving liability claims cheaply and quickly. Sealed-secret terms would be harder to enforce under this bill, making claims costlier to resolve, a cost that shows up in liability prices paid by consumers.
